title: The Psalms, again
tomorrow: Mark 1 moves fast. what's the little word that makes it run?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, and the line the road of beads, a worry walking beside his story. Today, a book of prayers far older than the beads.
screen: `THE ROAD OF BEADS.` → `OLDER THAN THE BEADS.`

segments.voice: A text at midnight: a friend's mom has surgery in the morning, and she can't sleep. You type something, delete it, type it again. Words run out fast at an hour like that. Camp one of this path ended with a promise: the Psalms as 150 doors, a way in for every mood. So which psalm do you send a scared friend at midnight?
screen: `A TEXT AT MIDNIGHT.` → `WORDS RUN OUT.` → `150 DOORS. WHICH ONE?`

segments.voice: When your own words run out, the Psalms lend you theirs. The shepherd psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, starts plainly: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing." And it doesn't pretend the night isn't dark: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me." Catholics sing a psalm at every Mass, the responsorial psalm, right after the first reading. But this book is shared ground. Jews pray the same psalm; in the JPS translation it begins, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Jewish tradition calls the book Tehillim, praises, and keeps a custom of saying psalms for someone who is sick. Same words, prayed in two houses, for the same scared nights. And one honest difference. Jews pray the Psalms as Israel's own songs. Catholics pray them too, and also hear Jesus praying them: on the cross, Mark says, he cried out, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", the first line of a psalm. One to tell a friend: you can even see the difference on the page. The shepherd psalm is number 22 in the Douay-Rheims and 23 in the JPS. Two numberings, one song.
screen: `WHEN WORDS RUN OUT.` · `THE LORD RULETH ME.` · `ONE SONG, TWO HOUSES.` · `HIS PRAYER ON THE CROSS.` · then, large: `YOUR PSALM.`

segments.voice: Say your psalm out loud, the one that has become yours on this road. If none has yet, borrow the shepherd's first line: the Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing. Say it slowly twice, once for yourself and once for someone who's afraid tonight.
The Psalms. Borrowed words for nights your own run out, prayed in synagogues and churches alike.
Your line: your psalm, the door you keep walking through, on easy nights and hard ones. Go in peace.

fork.reveal: shared ground, named honestly: the same psalms in both houses, and a real difference in how each hears them. no ranking, and no 'all the same'.

chat.meaning: The Psalms are shared ground: Jews and Catholics pray the same songs, numbered a little differently. A psalm is a fitting gift for a scared night.

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible

responsorial psalm.meaning: the psalm sung at Mass after the first reading, with a refrain

JPS.meaning: the Jewish Publication Society's English translation of the Hebrew Bible

Tehillim.meaning: Hebrew for praises; the Jewish name for the book of Psalms
